lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Excuse me, do you speak English?
lessons.goal: Ask if someone speaks English or understands Spanish, and answer yes, no, or a little

steps.n: Welcome to Brodoit Spanish. Listen to this conversation between an American man and a Spanish woman meeting on a street in Madrid.

He said: Excuse me, madam. Do you speak English? She answered: No, sir. I don't speak English. Do you understand Spanish? And he said: Yes, a little. In the next fifteen minutes you will learn to say all of that yourself.
Let's begin with the word for 'Spanish', the language. Listen, then repeat each part.
Now the phrase 'do you understand', or 'you understand'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is the polite word for 'you'. In Spain you use it with strangers and older people. Listen and repeat.
Spanish puts the word for 'you' after the verb in a question. Try to ask 'do you understand?', with the word for 'you' included.
Now ask 'do you understand Spanish?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask me if I understand Spanish.
Here is how to say 'I understand'. Notice the ending changes from 'eh' to 'oh'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is the word for 'no'. It is easy.
Say 'I don't understand'. Just put 'no' in front.
Say 'I don't understand'.
Here is 'yes'.
Here is the word for 'English'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'do you speak', or 'you speak'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Now ask 'do you speak English?' Remember, the word for 'you' goes after the verb. Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask her if she speaks English.
Here is 'I speak'. Again the ending changes to 'oh'.
Say 'I don't speak English'.
Say 'I don't understand'.
Say 'I don't speak English'.
Here is how to say 'a little'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'Yes, a little.'
Say 'I speak a little Spanish.' Say 'I speak', then 'a little', then 'Spanish'.
To address a woman politely you say 'madam'. Listen, then repeat each part.
And here is 'sir'. It is the same word without the final 'ah'.
Here is how to say 'excuse me' to get someone's attention. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'Excuse me, madam.'
A note on politeness: the words for 'sir' and 'madam' are used far more in Spain than in English. Adding them to 'excuse me' or 'no' is simply good manners, not stiffness.
Ask me if I speak English.
Answer: 'No, sir. I don't speak English.'
Ask me if I understand Spanish.
Answer: 'Yes, a little.'

steps.q: How would you say 'I speak a little Spanish'?

steps.n: Say 'Excuse me, madam. Do you speak English?'
Now listen to the conversation from the beginning of the lesson once more. You will understand everything.
In the next lesson you will learn to greet people, say please and thank you, and say where you are from. This is the end of lesson one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Good morning, how are you?
lessons.goal: Greet people, say please and thank you, and say where you are from

steps.n: This is lesson two. Listen to this conversation. A Spanish woman greets an American man she has met before.

steps.t: Sí, soy americano. Soy de Nueva York.

steps.n: She said: Good morning, sir. How are you? He said: Very well, thank you. And you? She said: Fine, thanks. Are you American? And he said: Yes, I'm American. I'm from New York. Let's start with a quick review of lesson one.
Ask her if she speaks English.
Say 'I speak a little Spanish.'
Here is how to say 'good morning'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'Good morning, sir.'
Here is 'thank you'. Listen and repeat.
Here is the word 'many' or 'much', used with 'thanks'.
Say 'many thanks', that is, 'thank you very much'.
Here is 'please'. Literally it means 'as a favour'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'thank you very much'.
When someone thanks you, you answer 'it's nothing', the Spanish 'you're welcome'. Listen and repeat.
I say: thank you very much. You answer 'you're welcome'.
Now, 'how are you?' Literally: how are you, politely. Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask me how I am.
Here is how to answer 'very well'. Listen, then repeat each part.
To return the question you say 'and you?'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'Very well, thank you. And you?'
Now say 'Good morning, sir. How are you?'
Here is 'American', for a man. Listen, then repeat each part.
For a woman the word ends in 'ah' instead of 'oh'. Listen and repeat.
A note on gender: in Spanish, words describing people change their ending. A man is 'oh', a woman is 'ah'. You already met this with 'sir' and 'madam'.
Here is how to ask a man 'are you American?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask a woman if she is American.
Here is 'I am'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I am American', if you are a man.
Here is the word 'from', or 'of'.
Say 'I'm from New York.' The city keeps its Spanish name.
Ask a man if he is American.
Answer: 'No, I'm not American.' Put 'no' before 'I am'.
Here is 'hello', for any time of day.
And here is 'goodbye'.
Spaniards usually say 'see you later' rather than 'goodbye'. Listen, then repeat each part.
'Good morning' is used until lunch, around two in the afternoon. After that you say 'good afternoon'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'good afternoon'.
Say 'you're welcome'.

steps.q: How do you ask a man if he is American?
How do you say 'I'm from New York'?

steps.n: Say 'No, sir. I don't speak English.'
Now listen once more to the conversation from the start of this lesson.

steps.t: Sí, soy americano. Soy de Nueva York.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to ask where things are, how much they cost, and to count to ten. This is the end of lesson two.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Where is it? How much is it?
lessons.goal: Ask where something is and how much it costs, and count to ten

steps.n: This is lesson three. Listen to this conversation. An American woman asks a man in the street for help.

steps.t: Perdone, señor. ¿Dónde está el hotel Palace?
Está allí, en la calle Mayor.

steps.n: She said: Excuse me, sir. Where is the Palace Hotel? He said: It's over there, on Mayor Street. She said: Thanks. How much does a taxi cost? He said: Five euros, more or less. First, a short review.
Say 'Good morning, sir. How are you?'
Say 'Very well, thank you. And you?'
Now, here is how to ask 'where is?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'the hotel'. Notice the little word 'the' in front, used for masculine words.
Ask 'Where is the hotel?'
Here is 'the street'. This word is feminine, so 'the' sounds different. Listen and repeat.
A note on gender: every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine, and 'the' changes to match. You will simply learn each word together with its 'the'.
Ask 'Where is Mayor Street?'
Here is 'over there'.
And here is 'here'.
Say 'It's over there.' You just need 'is' and 'over there'.
Ask 'Where is the hotel?'
Answer 'It's over there.'
Now, 'how much does it cost?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'a taxi'. 'A' for masculine words sounds like this.
Ask 'How much does a taxi cost?'
To answer you need numbers. Let's count from one to five. Listen and repeat each number.
Say 'three'.
Say 'five'.
Here is 'euros'.
Say 'five euros'.
Here is the very common phrase 'more or less'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'Five euros, more or less.'
Ask how much a taxi costs.
Ask where Mayor Street is.
Now the numbers six to ten. Listen and repeat.
Say 'eight'.
Say 'ten'.
Say 'ten euros'.
Say 'It costs eight euros.' Start with 'it costs'.
Say 'Excuse me, sir. Where is the hotel?'
Ask how much it costs.
Say 'Six euros, more or less.'
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: Perdone, señor. ¿Dónde está el hotel Palace?
Está allí, en la calle Mayor.

steps.n: Next time: food and drink, and how to order in a café. This is the end of lesson three.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — I would like a coffee, please
lessons.goal: Order food and drink in a café and ask for the bill

steps.n: This is lesson four. Listen to this conversation in a café in Seville, between a waiter and an American customer.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: The waiter said: Good afternoon. What would you like? The customer said: I would like a coffee with milk, please. Anything else? Yes, a beer too. How much is it? Four euros. Let's review first.
Say 'good afternoon'.
Ask how much a taxi costs.
Say 'Five euros, more or less.'
Here is the polite way to say 'I would like'. It is the word you use to order anything. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'a coffee'.
Say 'I would like a coffee.'
Here is 'with milk'. In Spain a coffee with milk is the everyday breakfast coffee. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'I would like a coffee with milk, please.'

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.expect: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: Here is 'a beer'. The word is feminine, so 'a' sounds like 'oona'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Remember: 'a' is 'oon' for masculine words, like coffee and taxi, and 'oona' for feminine words, like beer.
Say 'I would like a beer, please.'
Here is 'also' or 'too'.
Here is what the waiter asks: 'what would you like?' Listen, then repeat each part.
And here is 'anything else?' Literally: something more? Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask me what I would like.
Answer: 'I would like a beer, please.'
Ask 'anything else?'
Answer: 'Yes, a coffee too.'
Here is 'water'.
And 'wine'. Spanish wine is famous, so you will need this one.
Say 'I would like water, please.'
Here is 'how much is it?', the phrase for asking for the total.
Ask how much it is.
Answer: 'Four euros.'
Here is 'I want'. It is more direct than 'I would like'. Spaniards use it often, but with 'please' it stays polite.
Here is 'to eat'.
Say 'I want to eat something.' You know 'something' from 'anything else?'
Here is 'to drink'.
Say 'I want to drink something.'
Ask 'Do you want to eat something?' Use the polite 'you' form, which ends in 'eh'.
Here is 'the bill', or 'the check'.
Say 'The bill, please.'
A culture note: in Spain the waiter will not bring the bill until you ask. Lingering over a coffee for an hour is completely normal.
Say 'I would like a coffee with milk, please.'

steps.expect: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: Ask 'anything else?'
Say 'Yes, a beer too.'
Ask how much it is.
Say 'The bill, please.'

steps.q: How does the waiter ask what you would like?

steps.n: Say 'Thank you very much. See you later.'
Listen to the café conversation once more.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to ask for directions and take the train, the bus and the metro. This is the end of lesson four.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Where is the station?
lessons.goal: Ask for and understand directions, and buy a ticket

steps.n: This is lesson five. Listen to this conversation. An American asks a woman the way to the station.

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.n: He said: Excuse me, where is the station? She said: Straight ahead, and then to the left. Is it far? No, it's near. Five minutes. Thank you very much. A quick review first.
Ask where the hotel is.
Say 'It's over there.'
Say 'I would like a coffee with milk, please.'

steps.expect: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: Here is 'the station'. It is feminine. Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask 'Where is the station?'
Here is 'to the right'. Listen, then repeat each part.
And 'to the left'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'to the right'.
Say 'to the left'.
Here is 'straight ahead'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'and then'. You already know 'then' from 'see you later'.
Say 'Straight ahead, and then to the left.'

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.expect: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.n: Here is 'far'.
Ask 'Is it far?'
Here is 'near'.
Answer: 'No, it's near.'
Here is 'minutes'.
Say 'Five minutes.'
Ask where the station is.
Ask if it is far.
Here is 'the train'.
Here is 'the bus'.
And 'the metro', the underground.
Ask 'Where is the metro?'
Ask 'Where is the bus?'
Here is 'a ticket', for a train or bus. In Spain this word is also used for banknotes. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'for' or 'to', used for destinations.
Say 'A ticket to Madrid, please.'

steps.t: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.expect: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.t: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.n: Ask 'How much does a ticket cost?'
Answer: 'It costs eight euros.'
A culture note: in Spanish cities the metro is cheap and fast, and people are used to being asked for directions. A polite 'excuse me' first always helps.
Say 'Excuse me, where is the station?'
Say 'Straight ahead, and then to the left.'

steps.expect: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.n: Say 'No, it's near. Five minutes.'
Ask where the bus is.
Say 'A ticket to Madrid, please.'

steps.expect: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.t: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.q: How do you say 'to the left'?
How do you ask if it is far?

steps.n: Say 'I don't understand.'
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.n: Next time: telling the time, and the days of the week. This is the end of lesson five.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — What time is it?
lessons.goal: Tell the time, ask when something leaves, and name the days of the week

steps.n: This is lesson six. Listen to this conversation at a station.

steps.t: Gracias. ¿A qué hora sale el tren?
A las cinco. Hoy no, mañana.

steps.n: He asked: Excuse me, what time is it? She said: It's half past three. Thanks. What time does the train leave? At five. Not today, tomorrow. Let's review.
Ask where the station is.
Say 'Straight ahead, and then to the left.'

steps.expect: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.t: Todo recto, y luego a la izquierda.

steps.n: Say 'A ticket to Madrid, please.'

steps.expect: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.t: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.n: Here is 'what time is it?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'it's one o'clock'. One is the only hour that uses 'is', in the singular.
From two onwards you say 'they are'. Here is 'it's two o'clock'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'It's three o'clock.'
Ask what time it is.
Here is 'and a half', for half past.
Say 'It's half past three.'
Here is 'and a quarter'.
Say 'It's a quarter past eight.'
Here is 'at what time?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'does the train leave', or 'the train leaves'.
Ask 'What time does the train leave?'
Answer: 'At five.'
Here is 'today'.
Here is 'tomorrow'. The same word also means 'morning'.
Here is 'now'.
Say 'Not today, tomorrow.'
Here is 'in the morning'.
Here is 'in the afternoon'.
And 'at night'.
Say 'Tomorrow morning.'
Now the days of the week, starting with Monday. Spanish weeks start on Monday, and the days are not written with capital letters. Listen and repeat.
Say 'Monday'.
Say 'Friday'.
Say 'Sunday'.
To say 'on Monday' you use 'the' before the day.
Say 'On Monday in the afternoon.'
Say 'On Saturday at night.'
A culture note: Spanish days run late. Lunch is around two, dinner rarely before nine at night, and 'afternoon' lasts until about eight.
Say 'It's a quarter past eight.'
Ask what time the train leaves.
Answer: 'At five. Not today, tomorrow.'

steps.expect: A las cinco. Hoy no, mañana.

steps.t: A las cinco. Hoy no, mañana.

steps.n: Say 'I would like a beer, please.'
Listen to the station conversation once more.

steps.t: Gracias. ¿A qué hora sale el tren?
A las cinco. Hoy no, mañana.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to introduce yourself and talk about your family. This is the end of lesson six.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 — My name is...
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself and your family, and ask people's names and where they are from

steps.n: This is lesson seven. Listen to this conversation. Two people meet at a dinner party in Valencia.

steps.t: Hola, me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Sí, tengo dos hijos. Y esta es mi esposa, Laura.

steps.n: She said: Hello, my name is Carmen. What is your name? He said: My name is David. Pleased to meet you. She said: Delighted. Do you have children? He said: Yes, I have two children. And this is my wife, Laura. First a short review.
Say 'Good morning, sir. How are you?'
Ask a man if he is American.
Say 'It's half past three.'
Here is 'my name is'. Literally: I call myself. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'My name is David.'
Here is 'what is your name?' Literally: how do you call yourself? Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask me my name.
Answer with 'My name is David.'
Here is 'pleased to meet you'. Literally: much pleasure. Listen, then repeat each part.
A man can also say 'delighted', like this.
A woman says it with the 'ah' ending.
Both phrases are common. 'Much pleasure' never changes, so it is the safe choice if you are unsure.
Say 'pleased to meet you'.
Here is 'I have'.
Here is 'children', or 'sons'.
Say 'I have two children.'
Here is 'do you have', or 'you have'.
Ask 'Do you have children?' Remember where the word for 'you' goes.
Here is 'a daughter'.
And 'a son'.
Say 'I have a son and a daughter.' 'And' is the sound 'ee'.

steps.t: Tengo un hijo y una hija.

steps.expect: Tengo un hijo y una hija.

steps.t: Tengo un hijo y una hija.

steps.n: Ask me if I have children.
Answer: 'I have two children.'
Here is 'my wife'.
And 'my husband'. In Spain people also often say a more everyday word, but this one is understood everywhere.
Here is 'this is', when introducing a woman.
Say 'This is my wife, Laura.'
For a man you say 'this is' with the 'eh' ending.
Say 'This is my husband.'
Here is 'my friend', a man.
And 'my friend', a woman.
Say 'This is my friend, Carmen.'
Here is 'where are you from?' Literally: from where are you? Listen, then repeat each part.
Answer: 'I'm from Chicago.'
Ask me where I am from.
Say 'I'm from New York.'
A culture note: Spaniards greet friends with two kisses on the cheek, even when meeting for the first time in a social setting. A handshake is for business.
Say 'Hello, my name is Carmen. What is your name?'

steps.expect: Hola, me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo se llama usted?

steps.t: Hola, me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo se llama usted?

steps.n: Say 'My name is David. Pleased to meet you.'
Say 'This is my wife.' then add her name, Laura.
Say 'I have a son and a daughter.'

steps.expect: Tengo un hijo y una hija.

steps.t: Tengo un hijo y una hija.

steps.q: How do you ask 'do you have children?'

steps.n: Ask 'Do you want to eat something?'
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: Hola, me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo se llama usted?
Sí, tengo dos hijos. Y esta es mi esposa, Laura.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to say what you like and what you want to do. This is the end of lesson seven.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 — I like Spain
lessons.goal: Say what you like, what you want to do, and what you need

steps.n: This is lesson eight. Listen to this conversation between a Spanish colleague and an American visitor.

steps.t: Sí, me gusta mucho. Me gusta la comida española.
Me gustaría, pero no puedo. Necesito trabajar.

steps.n: She asked: Do you like Spain? He said: Yes, I like it a lot. I like Spanish food. Do you want to go to Barcelona? I would like to, but I can't. I need to work. First, a review.
Ask me my name.
Ask me where I am from.
Say 'I want to eat something.'
Here is 'I like'. Literally it means 'it pleases me'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'Spain'.
Say 'I like Spain.'
Here is 'do you like?' Literally: does it please you?
Ask 'Do you like Spain?'
Here is 'a lot', or 'much'.
Say 'Yes, I like it a lot.'
Say 'I don't like it.'
Ask me if I like Spain.
Answer: 'Yes, I like it a lot.'
Here is 'the food'.
Here is 'Spanish' describing a feminine word, like food. It ends in 'ah'.
Notice: describing words come after the noun in Spanish, and they match its gender. Spanish food takes the 'ah' ending; Spanish wine would take the masculine form you learned in lesson one.
Say 'I like Spanish food.'
Ask 'Do you like Spanish food?'
Say 'I like the coffee.'
Here is 'to go'.
You know 'do you want' from lesson four. Here is 'do you want to go?'
Ask 'Do you want to go to Barcelona?' 'To' a place is the sound 'ah'.
Say 'I want to go to Madrid.'
Here is 'I would like to'. It is softer than 'I want'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'I would like to go to Barcelona.'
Here is 'but'.
Here is 'I can't'.
Say 'I would like to, but I can't.'
Ask me if I want to go to Barcelona.
Answer: 'I would like to, but I can't.'
Here is 'I need'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'to work'.
Say 'I need to work.'
Say 'I need to eat something.'
Say 'I need a taxi, please.'
Say 'I like Spanish food.'
Say 'I don't like it.'
Say 'I would like to go to Barcelona.'
Say 'I need to work.'

steps.q: How do you ask 'do you like Spain?'

steps.n: Say 'I would like a coffee with milk, please.'

steps.expect: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: Say 'I like the coffee.'
A culture note: Spaniards love to ask visitors whether they like Spain, and the food in particular. 'I like it a lot' is always the right answer, and it is usually true.
Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: Sí, me gusta mucho. Me gusta la comida española.
Me gustaría, pero no puedo. Necesito trabajar.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to talk about what you did yesterday. This is the end of lesson eight.

lessons.title: Lesson 9 — What did you do yesterday?
lessons.goal: Talk about what you did, where you went and what you ate, in the past

steps.n: This is lesson nine. Listen to this conversation. A hotel receptionist chats with a guest.

steps.t: Fui a Toledo. Visité la catedral.
Sí, mucho. Comí muy bien y compré un regalo.

steps.n: She asked: What did you do yesterday? He said: I went to Toledo. I visited the cathedral. Did you like it? Yes, a lot. I ate very well and I bought a present. A quick review first.
Say 'I like Spanish food.'
Say 'I would like to, but I can't.'
Say 'On Saturday at night.'
Here is 'yesterday'.
Here is 'what did you do?' Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask 'What did you do yesterday?'
Here is 'I went'.
Say 'I went to Toledo.'
Here is 'I visited'. Notice the stress on the final 'eh'; that ending marks 'I did' for many verbs. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'the cathedral'.
Say 'I visited the cathedral.'
Here is 'the museum'.
Say 'Yesterday I visited the museum.'
Ask me what I did yesterday.
Answer: 'I went to Toledo.'
Here is 'did you like it?' It is 'do you like' with the past ending 'oh'.
Answer: 'Yes, I liked it a lot.'
Here is 'I ate'.
Say 'I ate very well.'
Here is 'I drank'.
Notice the pattern: 'I ate', 'I drank' end in a stressed 'ee'. 'I visited' and 'I bought' end in a stressed 'eh'. Both mean 'I did it'.
Here is 'I bought'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'a present', or 'a gift'.
Say 'I bought a present.'
Say 'I visited the cathedral.'
Say 'I ate very well.'
Here is 'last night'.
Here is 'a restaurant'.
Say 'Last night I ate in a restaurant.' 'In' is the sound 'en'.
Here is 'I spoke'.
Say 'I spoke with my friend.' 'With' you know from 'coffee with milk'.
Here is 'did you go?'
Ask 'Did you go to Toledo?'
Answer: 'Yes, I went to Toledo.'
A culture note: Toledo, an hour from Madrid, is the classic day trip. Spaniards will happily ask what you did and where you ate; food is always part of the story.
Ask me if I liked it.
Say 'Yes, I liked it a lot.'
Say 'I bought a present.'
Say 'Last night I ate in a restaurant.'

steps.q: How do you ask 'what did you do yesterday?'

steps.n: Listen to the conversation once more.

steps.t: Fui a Toledo. Visité la catedral.
Sí, mucho. Comí muy bien y compré un regalo.

steps.n: Next time you will learn to make plans with people. This is the end of lesson nine.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — Shall we go to the cinema?
lessons.goal: Invite someone, accept or decline politely, and agree on a time and place

steps.n: This is lesson ten. Listen to two colleagues making plans after work.

steps.t: Lo siento, esta noche no puedo. Estoy ocupado.
A las ocho, en el hotel.

steps.n: She asked: Do you want to have dinner with me tonight? He said: I'm sorry, tonight I can't. I'm busy. And tomorrow? Shall we go to the cinema? Perfect. What time shall we meet? At eight, at the hotel. All right. See you tomorrow. Let's review.
Ask 'What did you do yesterday?'
Say 'I need to work.'
Ask 'Do you want to go to Barcelona?'
Here is 'to have dinner'.
Here is 'with me'.
Here is 'tonight'. Literally: this night.
Ask 'Do you want to have dinner with me tonight?'
Here is 'I'm sorry'. Literally: I feel it. Listen, then repeat each part.
Say 'I'm sorry, I can't.'
Here is 'I am', for states and places. It is different from the 'I am' you use for where you are from.
Here is 'busy', for a man.
And 'busy', for a woman.
Say 'I'm sorry, tonight I can't. I'm busy.'

steps.t: Lo siento, esta noche no puedo. Estoy ocupado.

steps.expect: Lo siento, esta noche no puedo. Estoy ocupado.

steps.t: Lo siento, esta noche no puedo. Estoy ocupado.

steps.n: Ask me if I want to have dinner with you tonight.
Answer: 'I'm sorry, I can't.'
Here is 'and tomorrow?'
Here is 'the cinema'.
Here is 'shall we go?', or 'let's go'.
Ask 'Shall we go to the cinema?' 'To the', with a masculine word, blends into one short word.
Here is 'perfect'.
Here is 'we'll see each other', used for meeting up. Listen, then repeat each part.
Ask 'What time shall we meet?'
Answer: 'At eight, at the hotel.'

steps.t: A las ocho, en el hotel.

steps.expect: A las ocho, en el hotel.

steps.t: A las ocho, en el hotel.

steps.n: Here is 'all right' or 'agreed'. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'see you tomorrow'.
Say 'Perfect. What time shall we meet?'
Say 'All right. See you tomorrow.'
Here is 'the weekend'. Literally: the end of week. Listen, then repeat each part.
Here is 'do you do', or 'are you doing'.

lessons.title: Lesson 11 — Do you have anything cheaper?
lessons.goal: Shop for clothes, talk about prices, and pay

steps.n: This is lesson eleven. Listen to a customer and a shop assistant in a clothes shop in Madrid.

steps.t: Sí, claro. Esta es muy bonita.
Es un poco caro. ¿Tiene algo más barato?
Me la llevo. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?

steps.n: Good morning. Do you have shirts? Yes, of course. This one is very pretty. How much does it cost? Thirty euros. It's a bit expensive. Do you have anything cheaper? This one costs twenty. I'll take it. Can I pay by card? Yes, of course. Let's review first.
Ask how much it costs.
Ask 'Do you have children?'
Say 'All right. See you tomorrow.'
Here is 'a shirt'.
Ask 'Do you have shirts?' Shirts ends in 's'.
Here is 'of course'.
Here is 'pretty' or 'nice', for a feminine word.
Say 'This one is very pretty.' You know 'this is' from introducing a woman.
Now some bigger numbers. Twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, and one hundred. Listen and repeat.
Say 'Thirty euros.'
Here is 'expensive'.
Say 'It's a bit expensive.' Use 'is' and 'a little'.
Here is 'cheap'.
Here is 'cheaper'. Literally: more cheap.
Ask 'Do you have anything cheaper?' 'Anything' is the word from 'anything else?'
Say 'This one costs twenty.'
Ask me if I have shirts.
Say 'Thirty euros.'
Say 'It's a bit expensive.'
Here is 'I'll take it', for a feminine word like shirt. Listen, then repeat each part.
For a masculine thing, like a present, the little word changes to 'lo'.
That little word 'it' matches the gender of the thing you are buying. If in doubt, just say 'this one' and point.
Here is 'to pay'.
Here is 'by card'.
Here is 'can I?', or 'I can'. You know 'I can't'; drop the 'no'.
Ask 'Can I pay by card?'
Say 'I'll take it', for a shirt.
Ask if you can pay by card.
Here is 'big'.
Here is 'small', for a masculine word.
Say 'Bigger, please.' 'Bigger' is 'more big'.
Here is 'too', as in 'too much'.
Say 'It's too expensive.'
A culture note: haggling is not done in Spanish shops, but at open-air markets a friendly 'do you have anything cheaper?' is perfectly normal.
Ask 'Do you have anything cheaper?'
Say 'This one costs twenty.'
Say 'It's too expensive.'
Say 'I'll take it', for a present.
Say 'The bill, please.'
Say 'Thank you very much. See you later.'
Listen to the shop conversation once more.

steps.t: Sí, claro. Esta es muy bonita.
Es un poco caro. ¿Tiene algo más barato?
Me la llevo. ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta?

steps.n: Next time is the final lesson: a full review and a real conversation. This is the end of lesson eleven.

lessons.title: Lesson 12 — A real conversation
lessons.goal: Review everything and hold a full conversation in Spanish

steps.n: This is lesson twelve, the final lesson of this course. Listen to a long conversation between Ana, an American traveller, and a Spanish man she meets in a hotel bar. You will understand almost everything.

steps.t: Soy de Chicago. Me llamo Ana.
Sí, me gusta mucho. Ayer fui a Toledo y visité la catedral.
Me gustaría, pero no puedo. Mañana por la mañana sale mi tren.
A las ocho y media. Necesito un taxi para la estación.

steps.n: You heard: Good afternoon. How's it going? Very well, thanks. And you? Fine. Where are you from? I'm from Chicago. My name is Ana. Pleased to meet you, Ana. Do you like Spain? Yes, I like it a lot. Yesterday I went to Toledo and visited the cathedral. Do you want to have dinner with me tonight? I would like to, but I can't. My train leaves tomorrow morning. At what time? At half past eight. I need a taxi to the station. All right. Have a good trip, Ana. Thanks. See you soon.
Only four phrases were new. Here is the informal 'how's it going?'
Here is 'have a good trip'.
Here is 'see you soon'.
And here is 'likewise', the answer when someone says 'pleased to meet you'.

A note on formality: everything in this course used the polite 'you'. Young Spaniards switch quickly to the informal form with people their own age, but the polite form is never wrong, and nobody will mind.
Say 'Good afternoon. How's it going?'
Answer: 'Very well, thanks. And you?'
Ask where I am from.
Answer: 'I'm from Chicago. My name is Ana.'

steps.t: Soy de Chicago. Me llamo Ana.

steps.expect: Soy de Chicago. Me llamo Ana.

steps.t: Soy de Chicago. Me llamo Ana.

steps.n: Say 'pleased to meet you'.
Answer 'likewise'.
Ask me if I like Spain.
Say 'Yes, I like it a lot.'
Now let's go back to the beginning. Imagine you have just arrived in Madrid.
Say 'Excuse me, madam. Do you speak English?'
She says no. Tell her you speak a little Spanish.
Ask where the station is.
She says: straight ahead, then to the left. Ask if it is far.
Say 'thank you very much'.
At the station, ask for a ticket to Madrid, please.

steps.expect: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.t: Un billete para Madrid, por favor.

steps.n: Ask what time the train leaves.
Say 'At half past three.'
Ask how much a ticket costs.
Say 'thirty euros'.
Say 'It's a bit expensive.'
Now you are in a café.
The waiter asks what you would like. Order a coffee with milk, please.

steps.expect: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.t: Quisiera un café con leche, por favor.

steps.n: He asks 'anything else?' Say 'Yes, a beer too.'
Say 'I want to eat something.'
Ask for the bill, please.
Ask how much it is.
Say 'Can I pay by card?'
Now you meet someone at a party.
Say 'Hello, my name is Carmen. What is your name?'

steps.t: Hola, me llamo Carmen. ¿Cómo se llama usted?

Say 'I have a son and a daughter.'

steps.n: Ask 'Do you have children?'
Say 'I like Spanish food.'
Ask 'What did you do yesterday?'
Answer: 'Yesterday I went to Toledo and visited the cathedral.'

steps.t: Ayer fui a Toledo y visité la catedral.

steps.expect: Ayer fui a Toledo y visité la catedral.

steps.t: Ayer fui a Toledo y visité la catedral.

steps.n: Ask 'Do you want to have dinner with me tonight?'
Decline: 'I would like to, but I can't.'
Say 'My train leaves tomorrow morning.' Start with 'tomorrow morning', then 'leaves my train'.

steps.expect: Mañana por la mañana sale mi tren.

steps.t: Mañana por la mañana sale mi tren.

steps.n: Ask 'Shall we go to the cinema?'
Ask 'What time shall we meet?'
Say 'At eight, at the hotel.'

steps.expect: A las ocho, en el hotel.

Say 'I need a taxi to the station.'

Say 'See you soon.'

steps.n: You have finished the Brodoit Spanish audio course. You can greet people, order, ask the way, tell the time, talk about yourself and make plans, all out loud. Keep listening to Spanish, and repeat these lessons whenever you like. Goodbye, and have a good trip.
